name: Breton
confidence_why: Press 2009 (following his 1986 grammar), Ternes 1992, Bothorel 1982 and Kennard 2021 and 2024 all place Breton word stress on the penultimate syllable in the KLT dialects, with final stress only in a short closed list of words and throughout the Gwenedeg dialect; the one contrary line, a passing remark in Jouitteau 2005 calling KLT stress antepenultimate, sits in a syntax thesis and also calls French penultimate, so it is a slip rather than a rival analysis.
catalog_quote: Word stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable. (Ternes 1992)

new_statements.quote: Le dialecte vannetais du Breton, aux influences latines plus prononcées descendrait ainsi du gaulois quand le groupe plus homogène des autres dialectes du breton (cornouaillais, léonard, trégorois et gouelo : désormais KLTG) pourrait descendre plus directement du moyen gallois [...] Cette hypothèse est par exemple appuyée par les paradigmes de l'accentuation. Le français et le vannetais d'une part sont accentués sur la pénultième quand les dialectes KLTG d'autre part sont accentués sur l'antépénultième.
new_statements.translation: The Vannetais dialect of Breton, with more pronounced Latin influences, would thus descend from Gaulish, while the more homogeneous group of the other Breton dialects (Cornouaillais, Léonard, Trégorois and Goëlo: henceforth KLTG) could descend more directly from Middle Welsh [...] This hypothesis is supported, for example, by the stress paradigms. French and Vannetais on the one hand are stressed on the penultimate, whereas the KLTG dialects on the other hand are stressed on the antepenultimate.
new_statements.citation: Jouitteau, Mélanie (2005). La syntaxe comparée du Breton. Univ. de Naonded. Université de Nantes. 610 pp.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 1 (introduction, dialect history paragraph), p. 42 (page after the '41' footer; PDF page 43 of); clitic remarks pp. 74, 82, 91, 493

Full sentence: 'Cette hypothèse est par exemple appuyée par les paradigmes de l'accentuation. Le français et le vannetais d'une part sont accentués sur la pénultième quand les dialectes KLTG d'autre part sont accentués sur l'antépénultième.' Translation is faithful. Context is the dialect-genealogy paragraph of the introduction (Gaulish vs Welsh ancestry), a s…
new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the catalog's penultimate rule (StressTyp2: penultimate stress) as literally worded: it places KLTG stress on the antepenult and Vannetais on the penult. The work is a syntax thesis with no phonology section; the remark is a passing one and, given that French is called penultimate in the same sentence, it looks like an off-by-one description rather than a reasoned counter-claim. Compatible with the catalog only in the relative sense that Vannetais is one syllable further right than KLT.
new_statements.rule_in_words: As literally stated: the KLTG dialects (Cornouaille, Léon, Trégor, Goëlo) stress the antepenultimate syllable; Vannetais (and French) stress the penultimate. This is a single passing remark in a syntax thesis, made to support a dialect-history argument; it gives no examples and no domain (word vs phrase). Note that the same sentence calls French penultimate-stressed, which no standard description does (French is described as final), so both positions read as one syllable to the left of the standard picture (KLT penultimate, Vannetais final); the relative ordering (Vannetais one syllable further right than KLTG) does match the standard picture.
new_statements.exceptions: On clitics: the preverbal particle (rannig) 'est effectivement un monosyllabique non accentué' (p. 74), 'le rannig est monosyllabique et non accentué' (p. 82), 'Les particules préverbales et le déterminant présentent aussi la particularité commune de n'être pas accentuées' (p. 91); by contrast, citing Schafer (1997), 'Les auxiliaires en breton peuvent être accentués, ils ne sont pas tous monosyllabiques' (p. 493), i.e. auxiliaries are not clitics.
new_statements.identity_note: Jouitteau (2005) distinguishes Vannetais (Gwenedeg) from the KLTG group (Cornouaillais, Léonard, Trégorois, Goëlo) and gives them different stress placements; the catalog's single penultimate rule matches the standard description of KLT/standard Breton, not Vannetais (usually described as final-stressed). Hingant (1868) is a Trégorois-area grammar (Tréguier) and says nothing about stress. Kennard (2024), per its title, concerns the loss of stressed clitics in Breton prosody, i.e. change across speaker generations rather than a dialect.

new_statements.quote: For most dialects of Breton, stress is largely penultimate. [...] The KLT dialects have predominantly penultimate stress, as in, for example, á.val 'apple', ba.lá.fenn 'butterfly' or ka.ro.té.zenn 'carrot'. There are then a number of word-final exceptions; Hemon (1941) lists around 50 commonly used words with final stress in the KLT dialects. [...] Unlike the KLT dialects, gwenedeg has stress on the final syllable throughout, and the difference in stress pattern can be traced back to the period of transition between Old Breton and Middle Breton, around 1000 AD (van der Hulst, et al. 1999: 445).
new_statements.citation: Kennard, Holly J. 2024. Prosodic change in Breton: the loss of stressed clitics. Transactions of the Philological Society 122(2): 254-280.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (StressTyp2) records penultimate stress (penultimate stress); Kennard 2024 states the same default for most dialects (KLT) and adds: a closed list of ~50 lexically final-stressed words, the bimoraic-stressed-syllable condition, the clitic stress shift (indefinite article/numerals/re + monosyllable = one penultimate-stress domain) and its ongoing loss, and the dialect split whereby gwenedeg (Vannetais) has fixed FINAL stress -- a different placement for that variety, which the single catalog record does not distinguish.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the KLT dialects (kerneveg, leoneg, tregerieg = most of Breton and the basis of the standard) primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; monosyllables carry a single stress; about 50 common words (Hemon 1941) are lexical exceptions with final stress (e.g. pemóc'h 'pig', Pantekóst, fallákr, emáñ, ganín, some placenames). The south-eastern gwenedeg (Vannetais) dialect instead has final stress throughout. In KLT, certain function words (indefinite article ur/un/ul, cardinal numerals, eil, ken, pegen, pet, re) take the main stress when they precede a monosyllabic content word (ún ti 'a house' vs an tí 'the house'), i.e. clitic+host form one domain for penultimate stress; the definite article, possessives, particles and most prepositions/conjunctions never bear stress. Stressed syllables must be bimoraic (vowel lengthening in stressed open penults, e.g. pesked [ˈpɛskɛt] vs peskedenn [pɛsˈkeːdən]); unstressed vowels are short and may reduce to schwa post-tonically (kerneveg). The paper's finding: clitic stress is being lost, retained mainly west/north of a line through tregerieg and kerneveg, most eroded with the indefinite article, best kept with numerals 'two'/'three'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-internal secondary-stress rule is stated. The only mentions: Sommerfelt (1978: 96, St-Pol-de-Léon) describes the monosyllabic host after a stressed clitic as bearing a 'weak stress'; Kennard concludes (Section 5) that stressed clitics are affixal clitics with stress assigned postlexically and 'a degree of secondary stress remaining on the monosyllabic content word' (its vowel is short but not reduced).
new_statements.exceptions: ~50 commonly used KLT words with final stress (Hemon 1941): nouns pemóc'h, Pantekóst; adjective fallákr; situational forms of bezañ (emáñ); inflected prepositions (ganín); many function words; placenames Kastellín, Lokárn, Penhárz. Gwenedeg dialect: final stress throughout, no clitic stress shift (Ternes 1970, Ile de Groix). Unstressable function words: definite article ar/an/al, possessives (ma), preverbal particles a/e, prepositions like da, conjunctions pe, ha.
new_statements.identity_note: Kennard 2024 describes the KLT dialects (kerneveg, leoneg, tregerieg; her own pilot fieldwork is in south-west kerneveg) as penultimate-stress varieties and explicitly sets apart gwenedeg (Vannetais, region of Vannes/Gwened) as having fixed final stress; the corpus study (ALBB, NALBB, BSDB) covers all of Lower Brittany.

tone_statements.citation: Kang, Seongwoo. 2026. Beyond Phonological Labels: Tonal Alignment and Pitch Contour Variation in Breton. Paper presented at the Celtic Students Conference, Dublin, 11 June 2026. 23 pp. HAL hal-05652873, version 1.
tone_statements.quote: Firstly, Breton (except for south-eastern dialects, namely Vannetais 1 ) has acoustically realised stress. … Breton (except for south-eastern dialects where the most metrically strong syllable is described as the final syllable) has mostly fixed penultimate stress. … This has a phonological consequence on post-lexical pitch accents, as remarked in Kang [13] … Regarding Breton pitch accents, we broadly used two Tone and Break Indices (henceforth ToBI ) conventions within the autosegmental-metrical phonology framework [16, 2]. We observed H ∗ and LH ∗ pitch accents

tone_statements.citation: Elfner, Emily, Mélanie Jouitteau & Francesc Torres-Tamarit. 2025. Word Order and Prosodic Phrasing in Breton. Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 1(1) (issue: Proceedings of the 2023 and 2024 Annual Meetings on Phonology; Supplemental Proceedings). Amherst: University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. Published 24 March 2025. doi:10.7275/amphonology.3028. CC BY 4.0.
tone_statements.quote: This preliminary study investigates the interaction between prosodic phrasing and word order in Breton, focusing on neutral, broad-focus declarative sentences with various V1 and V2 structures. We identify the phonological phrase as the domain for pitch accent association. Breton phonological phrases have a single pitch accent and are generally right-headed, except when the second element is a function word (e.g., an auxiliary or copula), in which case only the initial word (S or V) receives the sole pitch accent or a more prominent one.
tone_statements.locator: Abstract, as displayed on the journal landing page openpublishing.library.umass.edu/amphonology/article/id/3028/ (first three sentences)
tone_statements.n_tones: No lexical tones; one pitch accent per phonological phrase (intonational)

tone_statements.citation: Elfner, Emily, Francesc Torres-Tamarit & Mélanie Jouitteau. 2024. Prosodic phrasing in Breton. In Minghui Dong, Yanfeng Lu & Ying Chen (eds.), East Meets West: Explorations in Tone and Intonation. Proceedings of the Second International Conference on Tone and Intonation (TAI 2023), Singapore, 18-20 November 2023, 77-78. Chinese and Oriental Languages Information Processing Society. (HAL hal-04636621, pre-publication version, CC BY 4.0.)
tone_statements.quote: We propose that the LH* pitch accent marks the right edge of a phonological phrase, and is placed on the stressed syllable of the prosodic word (w) closest to the right edge of this phrase. In most cases, each of the main components of the sentence (V, S, and O) each receive a pitch accent, suggesting that each w is parsed as its own phonological phrase (j) (see Tables 1 and 2). In Breton, lexical (prosodic) words are marked with a single primary stress, so when a syntactic phrase includes two lexical words, only the stressed syllable in the rightmost word will be marked with an LH* pitch accent.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 77-78 of the proceedings, paragraph beginning 'We propose that the LH* pitch accent'; '(w)' and '(j)' are the 's
tone_statements.n_tones: No lexical tones; 1 intonational pitch accent type described (LH*)

tone_statements.citation: Jouitteau, Mélanie (ed.). 2009-2026. 'Accentuation'. In ARBRES, wikigrammaire des dialectes du breton et centre de ressources pour son étude linguistique formelle. IKER, CNRS. Page version oldid=224982 (last modified 26 August 2025).
tone_statements.quote: Le terme d'accent tonique ne doit pas être compris comme induisant que le breton est une langue tonale. Il existe des langues comme le chinois mandarin où la hauteur mélodique ou la mélodie d'une syllabe est un phonème ou morphème à part entière. Modifier la hauteur mélodique modifie le sens du mot réalisé. Dans l'État français, la langue ndyuka qui est un créole parlé à l'ouest de la Guyane montre un système tonal ( Huttar & Huttar 1994 ). Ce n'est aucunement le cas en breton.
tone_statements.translation: The term 'tonic accent' must not be understood as implying that Breton is a tonal language. There are languages such as Mandarin Chinese where the melodic pitch or the melody of a syllable is a phoneme or morpheme in its own right. Changing the melodic pitch changes the meaning of the word produced. Within the French state, Ndyuka, a creole spoken in western French Guiana, has a tonal system (Huttar & Huttar 1994). This is in no way the case in Breton.
tone_statements.locator: ARBRES page 'Accentuation', section 4.1 'A ne pas confondre avec les langues tonales' (under 4 'Horizons comparatifs'), version oldid=224982

tone_statements.citation: Pilch, Herbert. 1990. L'intonation de la langue bretonne. La Bretagne Linguistique 6: 175-182. Brest: CRBC. doi:10.4000/lbl.7675 (online 5 January 2022).
tone_statements.quote: L'étude préalable (3) nous a conduit à poser, pour le breton, les deux accents distinctifs surnommés aigu et circonflexe, par exemple dans dèn 'dents' ≠ dên 'homme', àvèl 'vent' = mêvèl 'serviteur'. Chacun de ces deux accents survient ou bien comme figure montante ... ou bien descendante ... Les figures paraissent allophoniques du point de vue de l'accent - qui a toujours un certain degré de stabilité lexicale en breton, et cela veut dire de distinctivité. Or elles sont autonomes (c'est-à-dire distinguibles, pas distinctives) du point de vue de l'intonation...
tone_statements.translation: The preliminary study (3) led us to posit, for Breton, the two distinctive accents nicknamed acute and circumflex, for example in dèn 'teeth' ≠ dên 'man', àvèl 'wind' = mêvèl 'servant'. Each of these two accents occurs either as a rising figure ... or as a falling one ... The figures appear allophonic from the point of view of the accent - which always has a certain degree of lexical stability in Breton, and that means distinctiveness. Yet they are autonomous (i.e. distinguishable, not distinctive) from the point of view of intonation...
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Two lexically distinctive word accents ('acute', 'circumflex'); rising vs falling pitch figure is allophonic. What separates the two phonetically is in Pilch 1986, not here. At least 38 marked forms.

tone_statements.citation: Pilch, Herbert. 1986. L'accentuation de la langue bretonne. La Bretagne Linguistique 2: 43-68. Brest: CRBC. doi:10.4000/lbl.9368 (online 10 January 2022).
tone_statements.quote: Telle est la situation des deux accents du breton. Nous croyons que la différence mélodique entre eux est toujours présente, tandis que les autres paramètres proposés ne le sont pas. ... La différence mélodique que nous avons choisie comme trait pertinent s'aperçoit surtout par le mouvement abrupt (soit montant, soit descendant) pour l'accent aigu par comparaison au mouvement plus doux (soit montant, soit descendant) pour l'accent circonflexe. Pour chacun des deux, nous distinguons entre trois allophones, à savoir montant ..., descendant ... et (relativement) uni ...
tone_statements.translation: Such is the situation of the two accents of Breton. We believe that the melodic difference between them is always present, whereas the other parameters proposed are not. ... The melodic difference we have chosen as the pertinent feature is perceived above all through the abrupt movement (either rising or falling) for the acute accent compared with the gentler movement (either rising or falling) for the circumflex accent. For each of the two we distinguish three allophones, namely rising ..., falling ... and (relatively) level ...
tone_statements.locator: sec. 7.2 'La substance phonétique', facsimile pp. 12-13 (last paragraph) and (second paragraph); journal pagination 43-68 not printed on the facsimile
tone_statements.summary: Two accents (acute vs circumflex) per accent group, cued by abrupt vs gentle pitch movement, likened to Serbo-Croatian; author says others call it vowel quantity and its distinctiveness is elusive.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement: Jouitteau (2005: 42) states in passing that the KLTG dialects are stressed on the antepenultimate and Vannetais (like French) on the penultimate, which contradicts the catalog's penultimate rule as worded. Because the same sentence describes French as penultimate-stressed, the remark reads as a one-syllable-left shift of the standard picture (KLT penultimate, Vannetais final) rather than a considered counter-claim, and it comes from a syntax thesis without a phonology section; it should not displace the catalog record. Hingant (1868) is silent

sources.quote: We propose that the LH* pitch accent marks the right edge of a phonological phrase, and is placed on the stressed syllable of the prosodic word (w) closest to the right edge of this phrase. In most cases, each of the main components of the sentence (V, S, and O) each receive a pitch accent, suggesting that each w is parsed as its own phonological phrase (j) (see Tables 1 and 2). In Breton, lexical (prosodic) words are marked with a single primary stress, so when a syntactic phrase includes two lexical words, only the stressed syllable in the rightmost word will be marked with an LH* pitch accent.

sources.quote: Le terme d'accent tonique ne doit pas être compris comme induisant que le breton est une langue tonale. Il existe des langues comme le chinois mandarin où la hauteur mélodique ou la mélodie d'une syllabe est un phonème ou morphème à part entière. Modifier la hauteur mélodique modifie le sens du mot réalisé. Dans l'État français, la langue ndyuka qui est un créole parlé à l'ouest de la Guyane montre un système tonal ( Huttar & Huttar 1994 ). Ce n'est aucunement le cas en breton.

tone.translation: The term 'tonic accent' must not be understood as implying that Breton is a tonal language. There are languages such as Mandarin Chinese where the melodic pitch or the melody of a syllable is a phoneme or morpheme in its own right. Changing the melodic pitch changes the meaning of the word produced. Within the French state, Ndyuka, a creole spoken in western French Guiana, has a tonal system (Huttar & Huttar 1994). This is in no way the case in Breton.

sources.quote: L'étude préalable (3) nous a conduit à poser, pour le breton, les deux accents distinctifs surnommés aigu et circonflexe, par exemple dans dèn 'dents' ≠ dên 'homme', àvèl 'vent' = mêvèl 'serviteur'. Chacun de ces deux accents survient ou bien comme figure montante ... ou bien descendante ... Les figures paraissent allophoniques du point de vue de l'accent - qui a toujours un certain degré de stabilité lexicale en breton, et cela veut dire de distinctivité. Or elles sont autonomes (c'est-à-dire distinguibles, pas distinctives) du point de vue de l'intonation...

tone.translation: The preliminary study (3) led us to posit, for Breton, the two distinctive accents nicknamed acute and circumflex, for example in dèn 'teeth' ≠ dên 'man', àvèl 'wind' = mêvèl 'servant'. Each of these two accents occurs either as a rising figure ... or as a falling one ... The figures appear allophonic from the point of view of the accent - which always has a certain degree of lexical stability in Breton, and that means distinctiveness. Yet they are autonomous (i.e. distinguishable, not distinctive) from the point of view of intonation...

sources.quote: Telle est la situation des deux accents du breton. Nous croyons que la différence mélodique entre eux est toujours présente, tandis que les autres paramètres proposés ne le sont pas. ... La différence mélodique que nous avons choisie comme trait pertinent s'aperçoit surtout par le mouvement abrupt (soit montant, soit descendant) pour l'accent aigu par comparaison au mouvement plus doux (soit montant, soit descendant) pour l'accent circonflexe. Pour chacun des deux, nous distinguons entre trois allophones, à savoir montant ..., descendant ... et (relativement) uni ...

tone.translation: Such is the situation of the two accents of Breton. We believe that the melodic difference between them is always present, whereas the other parameters proposed are not. ... The melodic difference we have chosen as the pertinent feature is perceived above all through the abrupt movement (either rising or falling) for the acute accent compared with the gentler movement (either rising or falling) for the circumflex accent. For each of the two we distinguish three allophones, namely rising ..., falling ... and (relatively) level ...
